name: PT Mitrabara Adiperdana Tbk

frontmatter.title: Mitrabara Adiperdana — a cash-backed coal run-off the market prices for the end of the mine
frontmatter.summary: MBAP is a small North Kalimantan thermal-coal producer whose Malinau reserve runs out in 2028. The equity is mostly net cash plus a nascent non-coal platform; the coal business is a short annuity. At Rp1,695 the reverse DCF implies a Newcastle marker above the house deck's forward path but well below spot, and on the target's own post-liquidity basis the market is paying more than our value. We move to HOLD with a target of Rp1,658.
thesis: The reserve is the clock. Malinau holds 3.00 Mt of coal, the company plans to sell 1.45 Mt in 2026 and produce 1.30 Mt a year in 2027-28, and management says the mine ends in 2028 [S9][S10]. We model the run-off and assume no replacement mine in the base; the stated acquisition search is a free option, not a forecast.

The balance sheet is the value floor. Net cash, restricted cash, the solar joint venture and a non-coal platform carried at its sunk-capex floor together cover most of the current market capitalisation before any coal cash flow is counted [S4][S5]. The coal DCF is the swing factor, not the whole value.

The market is not pricing the house deck at a discount. The reverse DCF says Rp1,695 implies a Newcastle marker of about 122.8 dollars a tonne in FY2027E, above the deck's 118.0 forward path and far below spot 150.3, though above the long-run 105.0 [S3]. On the target's post-liquidity basis the price implies more still, so the coal price is not the source of upside we once thought [S0].

The base reproduces the last actual. Realisation is calibrated on FY2025A's own realised price, the DMO share is the disclosed obligation, the royalty is the IUP band the accounts show being paid, and cash cost holds the last actual in real terms [S4][S3]. No unsourced volume, grade or cost drift.

The strongest case against us is capital allocation, not geology. The US$105.0m 2026 capex programme is almost the size of the market capitalisation, 97.0% of it for subsidiaries, with no disclosed return target [S9]. A write-off there would erase most of the current market capitalisation.

The free float is 9.7% and the shares trade about IDR194.7m a day, so we carry the engine's 20% liquidity discount. At Rp1,695 the shares sit above the DCF after that discount; the peer-median cross-check is above the price but is the ceiling check and does not carry the target, so we rate HOLD [S0][S3]. The cross-check uses the peer median, not a blend, because the own-history mean is dominated by the FY2025 trough-EBITDA observation [S0].

blocks.text: We move coverage of PT Mitrabara Adiperdana Tbk to **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of Rp1,658, against a last price of Rp1,695, an expected total return of -2.2% with no dividend in the forecast [S0][S4]. The target is built from a life-of-asset DCF to the end of the Malinau reserve, cross-checked against a peer-median EV/EBITDA multiple, weighted across a bear/base/bull set and then cut for the stock's liquidity. It is not a bet on a coal re-rating. It is a cash-backed run-off in which the net cash and the platform floor are close to the price, and neither the DCF nor the cross-check, after the liquidity discount, now supports a higher rating. The earlier ADD rested on a blended multiple that put a trough-EBITDA year on a mid-cycle multiple; with that distortion removed, the rating follows the value [S0].

The company is small and the clock is visible. Malinau has 3.00 Mt of reserves left after the first five months of 2026, the approved 2026 production quota is 1.05 Mt, and management plans 1.30 Mt a year in 2027 and 2028 before the mine is exhausted [S9][S10]. Sales in 2026 are guided at 1.45 Mt, supported by coal stock left from 2025 [S2]. The in-ground reserve is the May 2026 figure; adding the coal already produced this year and our assumed stock draw gives a 4.05 Mt saleable base, which is what the model depletes [S9]. The stock draw is an assumption, not a disclosed tonnage: it is the gap between the sales target and the production plan, and the reserve total is therefore a modelling base rather than a company reserve statement [S9]. We model exactly that: a 1.45 Mt sales year in 2026, 1.30 Mt in 2027, and a final year in 2028 that exhausts the remaining tonnes; if the stock draw proves smaller, the final year carries less volume, which is the bear case's volume path [S9].

The variant view is about the price the market is putting on that run-off. At Rp1,695 the reverse DCF implies a Newcastle marker of roughly 122.8 dollars a tonne in FY2027E, about 1.04 times the house deck's 118.0; that is above the deck's forward path and long-run 105.0 but far below spot 150.3 [S3]. The price is also above the DCF after the liquidity discount, so the market is not paying "little" for the coal cash flow: on the target's own basis it is paying more than our value for it. The equity is not a deep-value anomaly; it is a cash-backed run-off whose DCF value, after the liquidity discount, sits below the current price. The peer-median cross-check sits above the price, but it is the ceiling check and carries the smaller weight; together with the bear and base scenarios it does not lift the probability-weighted target clear of the price [S0].

What moves the value, in order. First, the Newcastle and HBA path: every ten dollars a tonne on the marker moves the coal DCF materially because the mine has only three years left, and the deck itself puts spot well above its forward path [S3]. Second, the 2026-28 production and sales outcome against the RKAB quota: the stock draw is what lets sales exceed production in 2026, and a quota cut or a wetter year would remove it [S2][S9]. Third, capital allocation: the US$105.0m 2026 capex programme, 97.0% of it into subsidiaries, is the single largest use of the cash pile and the principal risk we now carry in the bridge; the thin float, not the capex, is the reason for the liquidity discount [S9][S3].

We do not ignore the bear case. The modelled bear cuts Newcastle by a fifth, sets volume to the approved quota every year and cuts non-coal revenue by a tenth; after the liquidity discount its target is below the current price, because the coal run-off and the platform, not the cash alone, carry the value [S0]. That is not a forecast that the shares must fall; it is a statement that the balance sheet cushions the operating downside but does not eliminate it. The write-off risk in the subsidiary programme is carried as a probability-weighted deduction in the bridge rather than left as an unquantified tail, and the free-float remedy is discussed in the risk section [S9][S5].

MBAP is one of the smaller listed Indonesian thermal-coal producers. Its scale means it is a price
taker in both the coal market and the domestic power market, and its equity is followed mainly for
its cash return and asset backing rather than for growth. The company has been diversifying into
biomass, solar and aquaculture in recent years, a strategy that is common among Indonesian coal
miners facing the energy transition but is still unproven at this company.

PT Mitrabara Adiperdana Tbk is an Indonesian thermal-coal miner listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in 2014, operating a single coal concession at Malinau in North Kalimantan under an IUP production licence [S3]. The mine has been operating since 2008 and produces a 5,400 kcal/kg GAR thermal coal sold into domestic and export markets [S3]. In FY2025A the company produced 1.95 Mt and sold 1.68 Mt, down from 2.27 Mt of sales in FY2024A as prices and demand softened [S3]. The concession is the whole of the coal business; there is no second mining asset in the base.

The revenue mix has shifted toward the non-coal businesses. FY2025A consolidated revenue was US$164.9m, of which coal revenue was US$136.1m and non-coal revenue was US$28.8m, the latter including coal handling, mining-contractor services and shrimp sales [S4][S3]. The coal segment still dominates, but the subsidiaries contributed 17.6% of consolidated revenue by December 2025 [S9]. The company reports in US dollars, matching the currency of its coal sales and removing a layer of rupiah translation from the operating line [S4].

The non-coal platform has four legs. Mining services are provided through subsidiaries including PT Baradinamika Mudasukses and PT Mitra Muda Makmur, with a contract book the company has described as worth US$53.5m to 2027 [S7]. Renewable energy includes the PT Malinau Hijau Lestari wood-pellet plant, with capacity of 150 ktpa, targeted for commercial operation in 2026, and a solar business with installed capacity of 12.8 MWp at end-2024 [S3][S7]. Aquaculture is run through PT Mitradelta Bahari Pratama, which has a shrimp production target of 1,800 t/yr [S7]. These businesses are small relative to coal but are the stated diversification route after the mine closes [S3][S6].

The customer base is Asian and domestic. The company sells to China, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand, Indonesia and Singapore, and the 2026 RKAB makes the domestic market the primary market [S3]. The domestic obligation is not a footnote: the DMO requirement was changed to 25.0% of actual production, and the company says it will comply with the 2026 RKAB [S3]. That domestic share is priced under the government's cap rather than at the export marker, which is why the realised price sits below Newcastle even before grade is considered [S3][S4].

Ownership is concentrated. PT Wahana Sentosa Cemerlang holds 60.0% of the shares and is the controlling shareholder, controlled by Ghan Djoe Hiang; PT Wahana Batubara Indonesia holds a further block above the five-percent disclosure threshold, leaving a public free float of 9.7% [S3]. The group structure includes the coal company, the mining-services and renewable subsidiaries, and the aquaculture venture, all consolidated [S3]. The concentrated register and the small float are central to how the stock trades and to the liquidity discount we apply in valuation [S0][S3].

Strategy is explicitly a transition away from a single commodity. Management describes the goal as becoming a diversified natural-resource platform, with the coal cash flow funding mining services, renewables and aquaculture, and with the company open to acquiring a new mine as Malinau depletes [S3][S10]. The 2026 capex budget is US$105.0m, of which 97.0% is for subsidiary development and investment [S9]. The company has not disclosed a return target for that programme, which is why we carry it at cost rather than capitalise a growth stream [S9].

Indonesian thermal coal is a large, policy-managed export industry. National production reached 790 Mt in 2025, and the government has said it will cut the national target to about 600 Mt to support prices [S2]. Indonesia is the largest seaborne thermal-coal exporter, so the RKAB quota revision is a supply shock for the seaborne market, not a marginal administrative change [S2]. For a small producer like MBAP, the quota is also a direct constraint: the approved 2026 production is 1.05 Mt against a sales target of 1.45 Mt that relies on stock [S2][S9].

Prices in the Indonesian market are set off the HBA and the ICI indices, not directly off Newcastle. The house coal deck carries Newcastle spot at 150.3 dollars a tonne, easing to 118.0 dollars in FY2027E and 105.0 dollars long-run, and HBA spot at 126.8 dollars a tonne with a FY2027E of 112.0 dollars [S3]. The domestic DMO cap is 70.0 dollars a tonne, and the company's 25.0% DMO obligation is priced against that cap [S3]. The grade matters too: Malinau's 5,400 kcal/kg GAR product is a mid-calorific coal, so its realised price is structurally below the Newcastle benchmark even in a strong market [S3].

The model prices the coal off Newcastle, not HBA, and the choice is deliberate. The reviewed deck carries an audited FY2025 Newcastle average but no FY2025 HBA actual series, so a realisation ratio calibrated on the last actual can only be fitted against Newcastle; fitting it to HBA would require a forecast-year ratio, the exact error the house method forbids [S3]. HBA is not ignored: the engine uses the deck's HBA path for the royalty tier and the DMO cap, and the HBA/newc spread is a stated risk. At spot the HBA sits at a discount to Newcastle, while the deck's FY2027E paths imply a narrower one; if the spread does not normalise as the deck assumes, the realised price is lower than we model. That is a signpost we monitor, not an input we can source a better series for [S3][S0].

Demand is supported near term by Asian coal-fired generation and by the war premium in the deck, but the long-run direction is energy transition. The company's own annual report describes continued demand from key Asian markets, constrained by softer global growth and the transition, with domestic demand stable under the DMO [S3]. The deck reflects that balance: spot is high, the forward path falls, and the long-run marker is below the forward years [S3]. That shape is exactly why we calibrate realisation on the last actual rather than on the spot spike, and why the DCF value is sensitive to the price path rather than to the current print [S4][S3].

Competitive position is weak on scale and adequate on cost. MBAP is a single-mine producer with 3.00 Mt of reserves and a three-year remaining life, against a national industry producing hundreds of millions of tonnes; it has no market power over price and no logistics moat comparable to the large integrated miners [S9][S2]. Its unit cash cost of about 60.5 dollars a tonne against a realised price of 97.7 USD/t leaves a positive cash margin before royalty, D&A and the non-coal cost base [S4]. The moat is the IUP itself and the domestic sales relationship, not the cost curve [S3].

The five forces are unfavourable in the usual commodity way. Rivalry is high because the product is homogeneous and the market is global; buyer power is high because domestic utilities procure under the DMO and export customers can switch; supplier power sits with mining contractors, fuel and logistics; barriers to entry are regulation and permits rather than capital; and substitution comes from renewables and gas over the medium term [S3][S2]. The one force that has moved in producers' favour is supply discipline: the RKAB revision is an explicit attempt to withhold supply and lift prices [S2].

Regulation is the dominant external influence. The royalty regime is the IUP schedule under PP 19/2025, which steps with HBA; the DMO is a production-linked obligation; the DHE export-proceeds retention rules tie up cash; and the government has discussed export taxes and the B50 biodiesel mandate, all of which raise costs or reduce cash conversion [S3][S2]. The company names DHE, export duty, B50 and RKAB restrictions as the main regulatory challenges [S2]. We model the IUP royalty band the accounts show being paid and the DMO share as disclosed, and we treat further regulatory tightening as a risk rather than a base-case cash cost [S3][S4].

External macro matters less than coal, but it is not irrelevant. The company reports in dollars and sells in dollars, so the rupiah translation affects the shareholder's return but not the operating margin; the house macro deck carries USD/IDR at 18,025 spot and 18,350 in FY2027E, with a balance-of-payments-pressure regime and a cautious tilt [S0]. Fuel is the main commodity input, and the deck carries Brent at 110.1 dollars a barrel spot easing to 84.0 dollars; the model passes a 15.3% diesel share of mining cost through that path [S4]. The house coal tilt is neutral, which is consistent with a name whose value is reserve life and cash rather than a leveraged bet on the coal cycle [S0].

The five-year record is a cycle in miniature. Revenue fell from US$449.5m in FY2022A to US$224.8m, US$217.9m and US$164.9m in FY2025A, as coal prices and volumes normalised after the spike [S4]. EBITDA followed, from US$16.7m in FY2023A to US$24.7m in FY2024A and US$8.6m in FY2025A, and net profit to the parent fell to US$1.5m [S4]. FY2025A was the trough: a small pre-tax profit, a high effective tax rate because of the small base, and a net margin of 0.9% [S4].

The FY2025A decline had two drivers. The company sold 1.68 Mt at an average realised price of about US$81.0/t, down from 2.27 Mt sold in FY2024A, so both volume and price fell [S3][S2]. Coal revenue fell to US$136.1m from US$172.9m, while non-coal revenue grew to US$28.8m [S4][S3]. The cost base did not fall as fast, so gross margin compressed to 10.9% and EBITDA margin to 5.2% [S4].

The first half of 2026 shows the recovery. Revenue was US$93.7m and net profit to the parent US$4.8m, with coal revenue of US$80.5m in the interim segment note and a stronger shrimp contribution [S5]. Operating cash flow was US$13.8m in the half, and the company held US$113.4m of cash on the balance sheet by 30 June 2026, drawing bank debt to fund the subsidiary programme [S5]. The interim result is consistent with our FY2026E forecast, which is why we have not pushed the base case above the company's own plan [S5][S9].

Our revenue build is volume times realised price plus non-coal revenue. We carry 1.45 Mt of coal sales in FY2026E, 1.30 Mt in FY2027E and a final year in FY2028E that exhausts the remaining reserve, at a realisation ratio of 0.78 to the house Newcastle deck held flat across the forecast [S9][S4]. The depletion base is the 4.05 Mt of saleable coal (the in-ground reserve plus coal already produced in 2026 and our assumed stock draw), not the in-ground reserve alone, so the 2028 plan is not cut by the stock accounting; the stock-draw component is an assumption and the sensitivity to it is the bear case's volume path [F35][F67][S9]. The ratio is calibrated on FY2025A: US$136.1m of coal revenue over 1.68 Mt of sales gives about US$81.0/t, which is what management confirms the company realised [S2]. With 25.0% of volume under the DMO cap at 70.0 dollars a tonne, the ratio solves the actual; it is not fitted to the FY2026E deck spike [S4][S3].

Costs hold the last actual in real terms. Cash cost is about 60.5 dollars a tonne, backed out of the FY2025A coal segment accounts after depreciation, mine-property amortisation and royalty [S4]. The engine applies the IUP royalty schedule for a 5,400 kcal/kg GAR product, which is the 13.5% band the accounts show being paid, and the DMO share is the disclosed 25.0% obligation [S3][S4]. SG&A and other operating costs are 9.4% of revenue, the FY2025A net figure including other operating income and taken net of its non-cash G&A depreciation because that charge is carried in the D&A line below [S4]. We do not add an unsourced strip-ratio creep or grade decline; the mine plan does not disclose either, and the reserve is exhausted on the company's own schedule [S9].

Depreciation is restated, not taken from the data pack. The pack's D&A is the G&A allocation alone, a fraction of the audited charge because IDX accounts use the direct cash-flow method; the fixed-asset note allocates total depreciation of US$8.3m between cost of revenues and G&A, and mine-property amortisation adds US$0.3m in FY2025A, giving a unit charge of about 5.1 dollars a tonne [S4]. Because the SG&A ratio is taken net of the G&A depreciation, the charge is counted once. That restatement lifts FY2025A EBITDA to US$8.6m and is the basis of the engine's calibration, which reproduces the last actual [S4][S0]. Cash cost is computed after the restated D&A, so the margin is not flattered by an understated charge [S4].

Tax is charged at the statutory rate, not the data pack's three-year average. The FY2025 tax reconciliation applies the applicable corporate rate to consolidated pre-tax profit, and the FY2024 line shows that rate is the statutory one; the 2025 effective rate is inflated by a small pre-tax base and non-deductible items, while FY2024's effective rate carries permanent differences [S4]. On our forecast that gives a tax charge of US$3.6m on pre-tax profit of US$16.3m in FY2026E, rather than the higher average the pack implies [S4].

Cash flow and working capital are the weak spot in the history. FY2025A operating cash flow was negative, and free cash flow to the firm turned negative (US$-45.7m), because working capital absorbed cash and capex rose to US$31.1m [S4]. We restate operating working capital to US$34.8m at end-2025, or 21.1% of revenue, from the audited balance sheet rather than the pack's inflated figure [S4]. The forecast releases working capital as revenue falls, which is why FCFF turns positive at US$12.7m in FY2026E and US$10.6m in FY2027E [S4]. Coal capex is held at about 3.0 dollars a tonne; the separate subsidiary development budget is treated as value-neutral at cost and sits outside the coal DCF, as explained in the valuation section [S9].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the story. At 30 June 2026 the company had US$113.4m of cash, US$40.0m of interest-bearing debt, US$186.4m of parent equity and US$11.7m of investment in a solar joint venture [S5]. Net cash is therefore roughly US$113.4m of cash less US$40.0m of debt, and a further US$7.3m of restricted cash sits outside the unrestricted balance, mostly DHE retention, which we add in the valuation bridge [S5]. Debt is bank lines and leases, with the MHL bank loan now largely long-term; there is no bond maturity wall [S5].

Capital allocation is the open question. The 2025 AGMS approved a FY2024 final dividend of IDR46.6bn, but the company paid no dividend in 1H2026 and has announced no FY2025 final dividend [S7][S5]. Our base assumes no distribution, with the cash directed to the US$105.0m 2026 subsidiary programme and the mine run-off [S9]. That is a deliberate choice: a resumed dividend would be upside to the total return, but assuming one without a declaration would violate the most-likely standard [S5][S7]. The dividend is therefore not in the valuation as a separate method; the dividend-yield cross-check is unavailable and dropped by the engine [S0].

Earnings-quality flags are mostly optics-class, not manipulation-class. The accruals ratio is not persistently high: FY2025A net profit was small and operating cash flow negative, but the three-year pattern reflects working-capital timing around a falling revenue base rather than fabricated cash [S4]. Receivables fell with revenue, but inventory rose to US$33.1m from US$24.7m while cost of revenues fell, a divergence the company explains by the deliberate coal-stock build that supports the 2026 sales plan [S2][S4]. The inventory note shows the stock is real and aged: gross coal inventory was US$33.3m at end-2025, against a coal-impairment provision of US$2.2m, and management states the provision is adequate after reviewing market prices and physical condition, with the stock insured [S4]. We treat the inventory build as an optics-class flag — disclosed, provided against and insured, but also the reason 2026 sales can exceed production, so a failure to sell it would hit cash and volume together [S2][S4]. The real structural flags are related-party revenue at 14.8% of consolidated revenue, a free float of 9.7%, and a controlling shareholder holding 60.0% [S4][S3]. The auditor is KAP Amir Abadi Jusuf, Aryanto, Mawar & Rekan (RSM), with an unqualified opinion on the FY2025A accounts, and no special-monitoring or special-notation status is disclosed in the filings [S3]. We classify the related-party and free-float issues as optics-class with a valuation haircut, not as a manipulation-class kill [S4][S3].

The reserves line in the table is the saleable base of 4.05 Mt (in-ground reserve plus coal already produced in 2026 and our assumed stock draw), not the 3.00 Mt in-ground reserve at May 2026; the difference is coal already mined plus the stock draw, which is why the 2028 sales plan is not cut by the stock accounting. Only the in-ground reserve is disclosed. The stock draw is an assumption derived from the sales target less the production plan, and the model's FY2028 volume falls mechanically if it is smaller [F35][F67][S9].

This is a commodity producer with a finite reserve, so the primary method is a life-of-asset DCF at the house coal deck's prices, not a multiple on current earnings [S4][S9]. The mine ends in 2028 on the company's own reserve and production plan, so the DCF has no terminal value and no growth assumption beyond the deck's price path [S9]. That is the correct frame for a run-off: a multiple on FY2025A trough EBITDA would capitalise a cycle position, and a terminal value would assume a mine that the company says will not exist [S9][S4].

The cost of capital is built from the house parameters. The risk-free rate is 5.0%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, the industry-median unlevered beta 0.80, levered to 1.02 at a debt/equity of 0.35, and a pre-tax cost of debt of 7.0% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of 11.8% and, at the market weights of 74% equity and 26% debt, a WACC of 10.2% [S0]. The WACC is used consistently across the DCF and the cross-checks; the engine's discount-rate sensitivity is in the table below [S0].

The DCF values the coal cash flows, then adds the non-coal assets and the balance-sheet items. The present value of the three forecast years is US$17.5m of enterprise value, the net cash position adds US$113.4m of cash less US$40.0m of debt, the solar joint venture adds US$11.7m, and the bridge adds a non-coal platform floor, restricted cash, a reclamation provision and a probability-weighted impairment of the unspent subsidiary programme [S4][S5]. The result is an equity value of Rp1,622 per share before the multiple cross-check and the liquidity discount [S0]. The DCF carries no terminal value and therefore no terminal-value share; the value is the reserve, the cash and the platform [S9]. The US$105.0m 2026 subsidiary development budget is not deducted at cost: the cash spent is converted into assets, but because the spend is far behind plan and no return target is disclosed, we carry an expected impairment of the unspent balance rather than assume full value [S5][S9]. The platform floor in the bridge is the already-sunk 2025 spend [S9][S4]. After the liquidity discount, the DCF-only value is below the current price while the peer-median cross-check is above it; the target sits below the price because the DCF carries the larger weight and the probability-weighted scenario set is below the price on the same basis [S0].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is Rp2,181, or 34.5% above the DCF, and we do not take it at face value [S0]. It now uses the peer median of 6.4 times. The previous draft blended that median with MBAP's own three-observation history, whose mean was dominated by the FY2025A trough-EBITDA observation; applying a mid-cycle multiple to a trough year and then to a three-year run-off double-counted the cycle and supplied most of the ADD. Both the peer median and an own-history mean that excludes the FY2025 observation remove the distortion, and on either basis the cross-check no longer lifts the target over the ADD band [S0].

Reconciled at the EV level, the gap is real: the peer median applied to FY2025A EBITDA of US$8.6m implies an enterprise value far above the US$17.5m the DCF gives the coal business. The divergence is not a hidden value gap. Peers carry longer reserve lives, diversified asset bases and different cash positions, and a mid-cycle multiple on a trough year is the wrong lens for a mine that closes in 2028 [S0]. The forward multiple on our FY2026E EBITDA, 1.5x, is the more relevant sanity check, and at the current price the equity is not cheap on it [S0]. We keep the method at the house weight as a ceiling check; it does not carry the target.

The industry card's other cross-checks either do not apply or are shown with their inputs. NAV at spot is the bull scenario, which holds the marker at the deck's spot rather than the forward path and is worth Rp2,436. EV/reserves is quantified at its two inputs: the DCF's US$17.5m of enterprise value covers a 4.05 Mt saleable base, so the reader can test any EV/reserve benchmark against it, but the ratio is cash-distorted and we do not anchor value on it. A cost-curve quartile cannot be sourced: no archived public AISC curve covers this single small mine, so we show unit cash cost against the realised price instead [S4]. The dividend-capacity yield is dropped because the company pays no dividend and has declared none [S0][S5]. The dividend anchor is unavailable as a fact about the company, not an omission by us. The price basis is Newcastle, with HBA used for the royalty tier and the DMO cap; the industry section sets out why the last-actual calibration can only use Newcastle, and the risk section carries the newc/HBA spread as a risk [S3][S4].

The weighted value is Rp1,786 before the scenario roll and the liquidity discount. The base scenario is worth Rp1,997, the bear Rp1,863 and the bull Rp2,436, with probabilities of 25.0%, 50.0% and 25.0% [S0]. We then apply the engine's 20% liquidity discount, which reflects a free float of 9.7% and a three-month average daily traded value of about IDR194.7m [S0][S3]. The result is the Rp1,658 target [S0]. The discount is large, but it is the right lens for a stock that trades this thinly; without it the target would be the pre-discount Rp2,073 [S0].

What the price implies is the core of the thesis, and it cuts against us. At Rp1,695 the reverse DCF solves to a Newcastle marker of about 122.8 dollars a tonne in FY2027E, roughly 1.04 times the deck's 118.0; that is above the deck's forward path and long-run 105.0 but below spot 150.3 [S3]. The market is therefore not pricing a modest discount to the forward deck; it is pricing a marker above it. On the target's own post-liquidity basis the price implies a marker at or above the deck's spot, because the discount we apply to our value is not applied to the market price [S0]. If the deck is right, our value is below the price; if the deck is too high, the net cash and platform floor limits the downside. That asymmetry is why the rating is HOLD, not a higher one [S0][S4].

The method set fits because the company owns a depleting asset and a cash pile, not a compounding franchise. A through-cycle NAV is the only way to separate the value of the reserve from the timing of the coal price, and the bridge is the only way to count the cash and the platform that the coal DCF does not capture [S4][S9]. The bridge also carries a probability-weighted impairment of the unspent subsidiary programme, so the largest downside risk is in the value rather than only in the prose [S5][S9]. The cross-check divergence is disclosed rather than smoothed, the multiple basis is the peer median rather than a blend, and the liquidity discount is applied explicitly rather than buried in a lower multiple [S0].

The largest downside risk is capital allocation, not the coal price. The company plans to spend US$105.0m in 2026, 97.0% of it on subsidiaries, which is almost the entire current market capitalisation, with no disclosed return target and a shrimp operation the accounts still describe as at the development stage [S9][S4]. The spend is also far behind plan: only a small fraction of the budget had been used by 30 June 2026, leaving most of it unspent but committed [S5]. If that programme earns its cost, the base case is intact; if it is written off, the equity would lose almost the entire current market capitalisation [S9][S5]. We no longer treat the programme as value-neutral at cost. The bridge carries a probability-weighted impairment of the unspent balance at a probability that is our judgment, not a disclosed figure: the company has published no impairment estimate and the record offers no base rate for a programme this early [S5][S9]. At the judged rate the deduction is already inside the Rp1,658 target; at twice that rate the target falls below the Rp1,695 price with the coal DCF offering little further cushion, and at half the rate it clears the price. The write-off is therefore a priced risk, not a tail we acknowledge only in words, and the probability is flagged as a judgment in the bridge rather than dressed up as a sourced number [S5][S9].

The second risk is the coal price and the deck's war premium. Spot Newcastle is 150.3 dollars a tonne against a long-run 105.0 dollars, and the forecast path falls every year [S3]. A return to the long-run marker early, or a wider realised discount for the 5,400 kcal/kg GAR product, would cut the coal DCF; the bear case models a fifth off the deck and, after the liquidity discount, takes the target below the current price, so the net cash no longer offsets the full operating downside [S3][S0]. The HBA/newc spread is a second price risk: the model prices off Newcastle because the deck has no HBA actual series, and if the Indonesian benchmark does not narrow toward Newcastle as the deck assumes, the realised price falls without any change in the Newcastle marker [S3]. The coal deck's tilt is neutral, and we do not assume a re-rating [S0].

The third risk is regulatory and operational. The RKAB quota is the binding constraint on 2026 production, the DMO takes 25.0% of output at a capped price, the DHE rules restrict export proceeds, and the government has discussed export taxes and B50 [S2][S3]. A quota cut, a royalty increase or a delay in the wood-pellet commissioning would each remove value [S2][S9]. The mine is also in its post-mining phase, with reclamation and closure obligations of US$4.6m provided on the balance sheet; a closure cost overrun is a direct hit to equity [S4].

The fourth risk is governance and liquidity. The controlling shareholder holds 60.0%, the free float is 9.7% against the exchange's 15.0% minimum, and the stock trades about IDR194.7m a day [S3][S0]. That combination means a minority holder may not be able to exit at the quoted price, and it justifies the 20% discount in the target [S0]. The float is a live structural issue, not a static one: the company discloses that public holders are below the threshold and that management is assessing ways to raise the free float [S3]. The listed free float is 119.1 million shares of 1,227.3 million; a placement sized to reach the threshold would issue new shares equal to a mid-single-digit percentage of the existing count, diluting minorities, and a discounted placement to affiliates would be a structure flag under the earnings-quality card [S3][S4]. Related-party revenue is 14.8% of consolidated revenue. We do not treat this as a manipulation-class flag, but the dilution path and the illiquidity are why the rating is HOLD rather than higher [S4][S3].

The fifth risk is FX and macro. The company reports in dollars, so the shareholder return in rupiah moves with USD/IDR, which the house deck carries at 18,025 spot and 18,350 in FY2027E [S0]. A stronger rupiah would reduce the rupiah value of the dollar cash pile and the target price; a weaker rupiah would help [S0]. The macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure and cautious, which argues for a discount to commodity beta rather than a premium [S0].

The scenarios shock the same three drivers. The bear case cuts Newcastle by a fifth, sets volume to the approved quota every year and cuts non-coal revenue by a tenth; the bull case holds Newcastle at the deck's spot marker and lifts volume and non-coal revenue, and the base holds the company's plan [S0]. The price leg is roughly mirrored in log terms around the deck. The volume leg is deliberately asymmetric and the asymmetry is sourced: the bear's volume is the RKAB quota disclosed for 2026, which is a hard constraint, while the bull's uplift is the company's own plan plus a modest allowance; the two cannot be a mirror without ignoring the quota [S9][S0]. A dividend resumption is not in the bull case because none has been declared; it is an upside signpost, not a modelled flow [S5][S7]. Probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull, reflecting a wide but not extreme operating range around a three-year asset [S0]. The scenario values are in the table; the base is Rp1,997, the bear Rp1,863 and the bull Rp2,436 [S0].

The signposts that would change the view are specific. A sustained Newcastle print below the deck's long-run marker, a widening of the newc/HBA spread beyond the deck's path, an RKAB cut below the approved quota, a write-down or impairment of the subsidiary assets, a dividend resumption, a free-float remedy, or a credible replacement-mine acquisition would each move the rating [S2][S3][S9][S10]. We would raise the rating on a dividend or a free-float fix that is value-neutral or narrows the liquidity discount; we would cut it on a write-off of the platform, a discounted placement to affiliates, or a quota cut that removes the 2026 stock draw [S5][S9][S4].

Ownership is concentrated and the controller is identifiable. PT Wahana Sentosa Cemerlang holds 60.0% and is controlled by Ghan Djoe Hiang; PT Wahana Batubara Indonesia holds the other large block, and the public free float is 9.7% [S3]. The company is part of a group that includes the coal mine, mining-services companies, the wood-pellet and solar businesses and the shrimp venture, all consolidated [S3]. The board includes independent commissioners, and the 2025 AGMS appointed a new independent commissioner after a resignation; there is no evidence of a special monitoring-board designation or special notation in the filings [S3].

Related-party dealings are material but disclosed. Related-party revenue is 14.8% of consolidated revenue, mainly mining-contractor services provided to affiliates, and related-party coal sales fell to zero in FY2025A [S4]. The accounts also show a loan and a pledge of subsidiary shares in the aquaculture venture, not of the controlling stake in the listed company [S4]. We treat the flows as a governance discount rather than a manipulation-class flag, because they are disclosed and priced, but they are part of why we apply a liquidity and governance haircut [S4][S3].

The audit is clean and the auditor is mid-tier. The FY2025A accounts were audited by KAP Amir Abadi Jusuf, Aryanto, Mawar & Rekan (a member of the RSM network) with an unqualified opinion dated 17 March 2026 [S3]. The company reports under Indonesian Financial Accounting Standards and in US dollars [S4]. There is no auditor down-tier change or going-concern language in the record [S3].

The dividend record is short and has just been interrupted. The 2025 AGMS approved a FY2024 dividend of IDR46.6bn; the company paid no dividend in 1H2026 and has announced no FY2025 final dividend [S7][S5]. The data pack shows dividends in earlier years, but the current payout is zero and our model carries Rp0 of dividends over the next twelve months [S0]. A resumed distribution is an upside case, not the base [S5][S7].

ESG exposure is dominated by the coal transition and mine closure. The company has a reclamation and mine-closure provision of US$4.6m on the balance sheet and is in the post-mining phase at Malinau [S4][S9]. It has a Green PROPER rating and is investing in wood pellet, solar and aquaculture as transition businesses [S3]. Those investments are the ESG story and the capital-allocation risk at the same time; the market will judge them on returns, not on the label [S9][S3].

The free float is the governance issue that matters most for a minority holder. At 9.7%, the stock is below the exchange's minimum free-float threshold, and the company discloses that management is assessing solutions to increase the free float [S3]. No specific remedy, size or price has been announced in the archived record, so the dilution path is a risk rather than a forecast: closing the gap with new shares would dilute minorities, and a discounted placement to affiliates would be a structure flag [S3][S4]. Combined with a controlling stake of 60.0% and a thin traded value, this is the main reason the target carries a 20% discount [S0][S3]. It is a structure flag, not a finding of wrongdoing, and we classify it as optics-class with a valuation consequence [S4].

The dated catalysts are the nine-month 2026 financial statements around the end of November, the wood-pellet plant's targeted commercial operation by the end of 2026, the FY2026 audited results and annual report in March 2027, the annual general meeting and dividend decision in May 2027, and the end of the Malinau reserve in 2028 [S5][S3][S7][S9]. Each is a checkpoint on the same three questions: how much coal is left, how much cash is left, and what the subsidiaries are worth [S9][S5].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are the monthly HBA and Newcastle prints against the deck and the spread between them, the RKAB quota and any revision, quarterly production and sales against the 1.45 Mt 2026 plan and the implied stock draw, the realised price against our 0.78 ratio, unit cash cost against 60.5 dollars a tonne, capex and cash against the US$105.0m budget, and any dividend, acquisition or free-float announcement [S2][S9][S5]. We also watch the wood-pellet commissioning and the shrimp volumes as the first real evidence on the non-coal platform [S3][S7]. A free-float remedy that is dilutive, or a second half in which the unspent capex is deployed on the same terms, would be the clearest reasons to revisit the rating [S3][S5].

The monitoring plan is deliberately simple because the asset is simple. If the coal price holds near the deck and the 2026 sales plan is delivered, the run-off generates the cash we forecast and the net-cash floor supports the rating; if the price falls or the quota binds, the bear case is the guide [S3][S9]. The one event that would force a full re-underwrite is a material write-off or a replacement-mine acquisition at a price that changes the reserve life [S10][S9].

bear.narrative: The war-premium carry in the coal deck collapses and the Newcastle marker runs 20% below the base through the three-year mine life; the RKAB quota stays at the approved 1.05 Mt every year, so 2026 sales fall to the quota and the stock draw is not repeated; and the wood-pellet/shrimp platform ramps below plan, with non-coal revenue 10% lower. The reserve is exhausted by 2028 and no replacement mine is acquired, so the equity is a run-off plus the non-coal floor.

bull.narrative: The war-premium carry persists at the deck's spot marker rather than fading to the forward path: Newcastle holds at spot through 2028, the approved RKAB is raised and the company sells the full 1.45 Mt in 2026 and 1.3 Mt in 2027-28 at the higher price, and the wood-pellet plant and shrimp ponds ramp to plan, lifting non-coal revenue 10% above the base. A replacement coal asset and a dividend resumption are not assumed: S10 discloses an acquisition intent with no price or reserve life, and no FY2025 dividend has been declared [S5][S7][S10]; both are upside signposts, not modelled cash flows.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: COMPANY PLAN, THEN RESERVE-CONSTRAINED. The company targets 1.45 Mt of coal sales in 2026 against a 2026 production plan of about 1.0 Mt (600 kt produced Jan-May plus 400 kt planned Jun-Dec), using stock left over from 2025 [F38/S9]; 2027 and 2028 production are planned at 1.3 Mt/yr to exhaust the remaining Malinau reserve [F37/S9]. The model carries 1.45 Mt in FY2026E (sales, including about 0.45 Mt of stock draw), 1.3 Mt in FY2027E and 1.3 Mt in FY2028E. Because the engine depletes reserves on sales volume, the reserve input is the saleable base of 4.05 Mt [F67]: 3.0 Mt remaining in-ground at May 2026 [F35] plus 0.6 Mt already produced Jan-May 2026 plus 0.45 Mt of stock, which supports 1.45 + 1.3 + 1.3 Mt of sales and leaves the mine exhausted at end-2028 as management states [S9]. No volume beyond 2028 is assumed.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: CALIBRATED ON THE LAST ACTUAL, NOT ON A FORECAST SPIKE. FY2025 coal segment revenue of US$136.08m [F34] over 1.68 Mt of sales [F1] gives a blended ASP of US$81.0/t, which management confirms was about US$81/t [F4/S2]. With 25% of volume under the DMO cap at US$70/t [F40], the headline ratio to the FY2025 Newcastle average (US$108.4/t, coal deck) that solves 0.75 x r x 108.4 + 0.25 x 70 = 81 is r = 0.781. The same ratio is held flat across the forecast; it is not fitted to the FY2026E deck spike of US$137.0. This is a medium-CV product (5,400-5,700 GAR) sold against HBA, so the ratio is a grade and DMO discount to Newcastle, not a margin assumption.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: The DMO obligation was changed to 25% of actual coal production for the year [F40/S3, AR2025 p.268], and management states the domestic market remains the primary market in the 2026 RKAB [S3, AR2025 p.104]. The engine applies the coal deck's standing US$70/t domestic-power cap (d.coal.dmo_cap) to that share. Some domestic industrial sales carry the US$90/t cap, so 25% at the power cap is the disclosed obligation rather than an assumption about the actual customer mix.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 so the cost block reads as a cost intensity (US$ of cash cost per tonne). No archived source in this window discloses the Malinau strip ratio, so the engine's cost_per_bcm is the coal cash cost per tonne backed out of the segment accounts.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Backed out of the FY2025 segment accounts so the model reproduces the year: coal segment cost of revenues of US$126.04m [S4, note 31] less the depreciation charged inside cost of revenues of US$6.24m [S4, note 25] less mine-property amortisation of US$0.34m [F11] less royalties of US$17.81m [S4, note 25] = US$101.66m of coal cash cost, or US$60.51/t on 1.68 Mt [F1]. Held flat in real terms and escalated with the coal deck's USD inflation. The non-coal businesses' costs are carried through other_revenue/other_margin, not here.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Fuel of US$15.54m inside FY2025 cost of revenues [S4, note 25] over the US$101.66m coal cash cost base is 15.3%. The engine lets the diesel component move with the oil deck (d.oil.brent), which is the correct link for a truck-and-shovel operation.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the whole coal cash cost (contractor, fuel, hauling, salaries, port and overhead inside cost of revenues) is already captured in cost_per_bcm at a 1.0 cost-intensity factor. Carrying a second per-tonne charge here would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Not used: the IUP licence reads the tier schedule from the coal deck (coal.royalty_iup_high), which steps with HBA. Kept at the 13.5% upper-band rate for completeness.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Non-coal revenue is real and disclosed: the non-coal businesses grew to US$28.80m in FY2025 [F33/S3] and the existing subsidiaries contributed 17.6% of consolidated revenue [F43/S9]. The base holds it flat because the company gives no revenue target for the new wood-pellet, shrimp and solar capacity; the 2026 US$105m capex programme is treated as value-neutral at cost (cash converted into assets of equal worth), so it neither adds a speculative growth stream nor subtracts the cash twice. The bear and bull cases flex this line.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Consolidated non-coal gross margin: FY2025 other revenue of US$28.79m net of eliminations [F33] against non-coal cost of revenues of US$20.85m (consolidated cost of revenues US$146.89m [F7] less coal segment cost of revenues US$126.04m [S4, note 31]) = 27.6% [S4]. This blends a profitable mining-services business with a loss-making shrimp operation; it is the disclosed consolidated figure, not a segment guess.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total fixed-asset depreciation of US$8.253m (US$6.237m charged to cost of revenues plus US$2.016m to G&A, the Note 11 allocation total) [F9] plus mine-property amortisation of US$0.336m [F11] = US$8.589m over 1.68 Mt [F1] = US$5.11/t. The data pack's US$2.02m D&A is the G&A allocation alone; the restated history reads the Note 11 total and the forecast carries the full charge, including the ongoing mine-property amortisation. Held flat in real terms.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Coal-only sustaining capex. The 2026 capex budget is US$105m, of which 97% is for subsidiary development and investment [F41/S9], leaving roughly US$3.2m for the coal business against 1.05 Mt of production [F36], or US$3.0/t. The FY2025 consolidated capex of US$31.12m [F24] is not a coal rate: 67% went to renewable-energy development [F42/S9], and the rest sits in the subsidiaries whose value is carried in the bridge.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero. The US$105m 2026 subsidiary capex programme [F41/S9] is treated as value-neutral at cost: the cash is converted into assets of equal carrying value, so the non-coal platform is valued separately in valuation.bridge rather than by deducting the spend and guessing its return. This keeps the coal DCF a coal DCF and avoids double counting the same cash.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: RESTATED. The data pack's NWC of US$103.13m is built on its understated cash line: it treats the omitted US$69.0m of cash as a non-cash current asset. On the audited balance sheet, non-cash current assets at 31 Dec 2025 were US$61.87m and non-debt current liabilities US$27.03m, so operating working capital was US$34.83m [F56/S4], or 0.2095 of US$164.87m revenue [F5]. The forecast uses 0.211 (rounded up, immaterial). As revenue falls in 2027-28 this releases the real coal inventory and receivable unwind, not a fictitious US$69m of cash.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: STATUTORY RATE, SOURCED TO THE LK. The FY2025 tax reconciliation [S4, note 16d] applies the applicable corporate income tax rate to consolidated profit before tax: US$5.473m on US$24.877m of FY2024 PBT, i.e. 22.0%, the Indonesian statutory rate. The FY2024 effective rate of 23.0% includes permanent differences and the sales adjustment under PP 15/2022; the forecast uses the statutory rate rather than the data pack's 33.0% three-year average, which is inflated by FY2025's small pre-tax base and non-deductible items. A profitable forecast year reverts to the statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 3.5%. The engine default of 15.0% divides FY2025 interest by FY2024 year-end debt, before the US$28.0m MHL bank loan was drawn. FY2025 finance costs of US$0.60m [F30] on average debt of about US$18.8m and 1H2026 finance costs of US$0.46m on about US$37m point to a 2.5-3.2% rate; 3.5% allows for the higher 2026 debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 3.5%. FY2025 finance income of US$3.43m [F31] on average cash of about US$114m, and 1H2026 finance income of US$1.92m on about US$109m, both imply roughly 3.0-3.5%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero. The 30 June 2026 balance sheet already carries the MHL loan [F18]; the model does not add new debt for the subsidiary capex programme because the programme is treated as value-neutral and the group's net cash position funds it.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Engine default constant; no separately forecast non-operating item.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero. The only material minority is 25% of the shrimp subsidiary MBP, which is loss-making, and FY2025 minority profit was negative [S0]. The engine default average is also zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. No FY2025 final dividend was declared and no dividend was paid in 1H2026 [S5 cash flow], after FY2024's Rp46.64bn distribution [F47/S7]. With a US$105m 2026 capex programme [F41] and a 3 Mt reserve, the most likely path is no distribution until the investment programme is funded; a resumed payout is an upside case, not the base.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Engine default constant; no rights issue or buyback announced.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Not used by the primary life-of-asset DCF, which ends when the Malinau reserve is exhausted in 2028 and carries no terminal value [F35/F37/S9]. Set at the house USD nominal long-run rate so the input is explicit and reviewed; any other vintages of the model that fall back to a terminal value use a coherent nominal growth rate rather than the engine default.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net operating expenses: selling expenses of US$13.19m [F32] plus G&A of US$11.23m less other operating income of US$6.82m = US$17.60m [S4, p.3], less the US$2.02m of G&A depreciation [F9] because depreciation is charged separately through the da line, = US$15.58m over revenue of US$164.87m [F5] = 9.45%. Held flat; the line already nets the recurring other operating income. Excluding the non-cash G&A charge is what lets the build reproduce the filing's EBITDA.

challenges.challenge: The 14.82x cross-check multiple is the average of the 6.44x peer median and a 23.21x own-history mean built from only three observations (FY2025A 48.61x, FY2024A 7.57x, FY2023A 13.45x). The FY2025 observation sits just under the engine's 50x cap and is a trough-EBITDA artefact. Applied to FY2025A EBITDA of $6.61m it values coal EV at $98.0m against the DCF's $15.7m. Replacing the blend with the peer median gives a target of ~Rp1,746 (+3.0%); excluding only the FY2025 observation gives ~Rp1,799 (+6.1%). Both are below the ADD band. The report concedes the double-count but keeps the 29% weight.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt on the peer median only (valuation.multiple_source). The blend put a trough-EBITDA year on a mid-cycle multiple and supplied most of the ADD. An own-history mean excluding the FY2025A observation removes that distortion but still values the run-off above the peer benchmark; neither basis clears the ADD band after the liquidity discount, so the rating follows the value to HOLD. The EV-level reconciliation is now in section 4.

challenges.challenge: At the EV level the cross-check values the coal business at $98.0m versus $15.7m in the DCF, a 6.2x gap. The "66.8% above the DCF" headline is a value-level comparison that adds the same $107.5m of net cash, platform and associates to both methods, so it understates the divergence the review must test. The industry card also prescribes NAV at spot, cost-curve quartile, dividend-capacity yield and EV/reserves; none is shown.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now reconciles at the EV level: the peer multiple's implied EV is shown against the DCF's EV and the gap is attributed to peer reserve life, asset mix and the trough-year metric. The card's other anchors are addressed: NAV at spot is the bull scenario; the cost-curve quartile cannot be sourced for a single small mine, so unit cash cost versus realised price is shown instead; EV/reserves is embedded in the life-of-asset DCF and is cash-distorted; the dividend-capacity yield is unavailable because payout is zero.

challenges.challenge: F67 records reserves as 4.05 Mt [S9], but the attached S9 quote says "cadangan batu bara ... sekitar 3 juta ton". The 0.6 Mt Jan-May production is in S9; the 0.45 Mt stock draw is not disclosed anywhere and is a plug: 4.05 = 1.45 + 1.30 + 1.30 exactly. The reserve is load-bearing for the FY2028 terminal year. Inventory rose 34% to $33.1m while COGS fell 14% [S4], the earnings-quality flag that funds the bridge is not addressed.
challenges.answer: F67 is relabelled a derived saleable-base assumption: only the 3.0 Mt in-ground reserve is disclosed, and the 0.45 Mt stock draw is the sales target less the production plan, not a company tonnage. Inventory quality is now sourced from the note: gross coal inventory, the coal-impairment provision, management's adequacy statement and insurance cover. The smaller-stock-draw case is the bear's quota-bound volume path, so FY2028 volume falls mechanically if the draw is smaller.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says the RKAB quota is "pushing 2026 sales to the quota" (1.05 Mt), but the modelled shock is volume x0.95 (1.38 Mt), a 5% cut versus the ~28% cut described. The bear is therefore not the quota-bound case the prose claims, and its claimed cushion is overstated. The bull narrative has the same problem in reverse: it says the company sells the full 1.45 Mt plan, which the base already does.
challenges.answer: The bear now sets volume to the approved 1.05 Mt quota in every year (op set), and the bear narrative says the quota binds and the stock draw is not repeated. The bull keeps the plan plus a modest uplift. The volume legs are therefore not mirrored, and section 5 states why: the bear volume is the disclosed RKAB constraint, not a symmetric shock.

challenges.challenge: Only $8.1m of the $105m 2026 capex budget was spent in 1H2026 [S5 p.11], so ~$97m of the $113.4m June cash is unspent but committed. The base treats the programme as value-neutral at cost (house-compliant), but §5 calls a write-off "the strongest argument against the rating" and the bear carries no impairment. A 15% impairment (~$14.6m, ~Rp214/share) takes the target to ~Rp1,747; 30% to ~Rp1,547, below the price.
challenges.answer: Added a probability-weighted impairment to the valuation bridge: 15% of the US$96.9m unspent at 30 June 2026 (the US$105m budget less US$8.1m spent in 1H2026), so the risk is in every scenario's value, not only in prose. Section 5 states that impairments of about a sixth to a third of the unspent balance take the target below the current price, and the larger case leaves little coal-DCF cushion. The spend pace and budget are sourced.

challenges.challenge: The free float is 9.7% against a 15% minimum, a 5.3pp gap with a 31 March 2029 deadline in the registry. The report says only that no remedy has been announced; the bear has no discounted-placement or dilution path, and the index/float consequences for a 60%-held name are not quantified.
challenges.answer: Added the share facts (listed free-float shares, total shares, IDX 15% minimum) and the company's disclosure that management is assessing ways to raise the float. Section 5 carries the dilution path: a placement sized to close the gap issues new shares equal to a mid-single-digit percentage of the existing count, and a discounted placement to affiliates is a structure flag. The engine has no share-count or bridge shock, so the path sits in the risk section and signposts rather than in the scenario table.

challenges.challenge: S10 (21 May 2026) reports MBAP is ready to acquire a new mine as Malinau depletes, with $113.4m of net cash and a life ending in 2028. The bull assumes no replacement asset and only +10% non-coal revenue. A life-extending acquisition is the obvious bull case and is treated only as a monitoring signpost.
